newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: High Irish April credit growth raises rate fears.
newsitem.headline: High Irish April credit growth raises rate fears.

text.p: Ireland's demand for credit continued to rise in April, fanning fears of an interest rate rise, but some economists felt a further catalyst was necessary to prompt the central bank to raise rates.
Ireland's adjusted annual private sector credit growth rose to 19 percent in April from 18.6 percent the previous month, central bank monthly statistics showed on Thursday.

The countries official external reserves fell by 20 percent or 1.13 billion punts to 4.74 billion punts, highlighting the authorities high level of foreign exchange intervention in the face of extreme volatility in the Irish pound over the last weeks.

"It needs a further catalyst for the central bank to raise rates," Irish Intercontinental Bank economist Austin Hughes told Reuters. Hughes said he saw the credit numbers as a smokescreen used by the Bank to hide concerns about the currency.

Riada economist Dan McLaughlin said the likelihood of another rate rise after Ireland's June 6 election was quite high but all economists agreed the currency was the real issue and would be the ultimate spur to force the central bank's hand.

"I don't think the slight acceleration in the rate of growth of the credit figures will of itself lead to any tightening of interest rates, the currency is what we have to look at," AIB Capital Markets economist John Beggs said.
"Support for the market at the end of April was well over a billion punts," Riada's McLaughlin said. "In other words the central bank was injecting well over a billion to keep interest rates down."
He said the Short Term Facility Rate (STF), which was raised by 50 basis points to 6.75 percent on May 1, was raised because the weight of selling in the punt was so great.
"The Bank spent a billion and then gave up and the punt plunged so they gave up and raised rates," McLaughlin said.
He did not think any of that pressure had gone away and said any time the punt touches 2.60 marks it will run into further selling.
The Irish pound has suffered severe bouts of selling on speculation that Ireland will want to enter a single currency at its central Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) rate of 2.41 marks.
This has caused the punt to drop up to 15 pfennigs in some of its sharper sell-offs.

Convergence activity slowed of late as uncertainty about EMU going ahead mounted, sparked by a row between the Bundesbank and the German government over gold revaluation and compounded by concern over the election of a Socialist government in France.
Currency dealers believe that once EMU looks set to go ahead again the punt will take a further battering.
AIB's Beggs said Ireland's inflation number for May will be key.

"If we saw a higher-than-expected CPI (consumer price index) figure for May then you would have expectations in the market place that the sterling/Irish rate couldn't go much below 90 pence without having an upward movement of market rates."

Beggs said Thursday's credit growth figures will not help "in settling the market's nerves over the inflation risks" but the fact that mortgage lending was unchanged at 14.3 percent may offer some comfort
"...but the overall figures remain extremely strong and of concern," he added.
